report.source_text: Magnetic resonance imaging indicated multiple hyperintense subcortical, and periventricular lesions visible on the fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) and T2-weighted images, in addition to bilaterally involving PPRF at the level of the pons, anterior to the cerebral aqueduct (Figs. 1-a, b). Two hyperintense lesions were also presented in the sagittal sections of the spinal MRI, one at the level of C7 and the other adjacent to T4. The lesions visible on the MRI were consistent with demyelination. After gadolinium injection, the PPRF lesions were not enhanced, however, T4 thoracic spine lesion was enhanced.

report.source_text: Considering physical examination, the patient had complete bilateral horizontal gaze palsy in the horizontal plane while vertical gaze was normal, aside from slightly decreased velocity of saccadic movements. Pupils were midsize and reactive, and nystagmus, diplopia or blurry vision were not found. Mild bilateral peripheral facial nerve palsy was also presented in the physical exam. Hyperreflexia in all four limbs was detectable without clonus, plantar reflexes were down going, and muscle forces were not reduced. There were no apparent signs of spasticity and ataxia. All other physical exam findings were normal.

clinician.final_diagnosis: diagnosis of MS was made in terms of the 2017 revised McDonald’s criteria
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 16-year-old girl presented with acute bilateral horizontal gaze palsy and a history of progressive paresthesia. Brain and spinal MRI revealed multiple demyelinating lesions, including subcortical, periventricular, pontine (PPRF), and spinal (C7, T4) lesions. The presence of both enhancing (T4) and non-enhancing (PPRF) lesions demonstrated dissemination in time. Serology for AQP4 and MOG antibodies was negative, ruling out NMOSD and MOGAD. Neurological examination confirmed gaze palsy, mild facial nerve palsy, and hyperreflexia. The patient responded well to intravenous methylprednisolone, with significant improvement in eye movements within a week and complete recovery by one month. The clinical presentation, MRI findings demonstrating dissemination in space and time, and exclusion of alternative diagnoses supported the diagnosis of MS according to the 2017 McDonald's criteria.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with acute bilateral horizontal gaze palsy and a history of paresthesia, indicating multiple clinical attacks.
Brain MRI showed multiple hyperintense subcortical, periventricular, and pontine (PPRF) lesions, consistent with demyelination.
Spinal MRI showed two hyperintense lesions at C7 and T4, consistent with demyelination.
MRI findings demonstrated dissemination in time, with an enhancing T4 thoracic spine lesion and non-enhancing PPRF lesions.
Serum AQP4 and MOG antibodies were negative, ruling out neuromyelitis optica and MOG antibody disease.
Neurological examination confirmed complete bilateral horizontal gaze palsy, mild bilateral peripheral facial nerve palsy, and hyperreflexia.
The patient showed significant clinical improvement in eye movements after treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone.
